questions.title: System bus
questions.text: Define the term **system bus** and name the components it connects.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Set of parallel wires / lines that transfer signals / data (1)
- connecting the CPU, main memory and I/O controllers (1)
scheme.model_answer: A set of parallel wires on the motherboard that carries data, addresses and control signals between the CPU, main memory and I/O controllers.

questions.title: Which bus?
questions.text: Tick (✓) one bus for each statement.

prefill: Carries the memory read and memory write signals
Carries an instruction from memory to the CPU
Its width decides how many memory locations can be used
Carries the clock and interrupt signals

scheme.mark_scheme: Control; address; data; address; control (1 each)

questions.title: Purposes of the buses
questions.text: Describe the purpose of each bus.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data: carries data / instructions between CPU, memory and I/O in both directions (1). Address: carries the address of the location to read from / write to, from the CPU (1). Control: carries control / timing signals e.g. read, write, clock, interrupt (1)
scheme.model_answer: Data bus: moves data and instructions between components in both directions. Address bus: carries the address of the memory location being used. Control bus: carries signals such as memory read, memory write and the clock.

questions.title: Direction of the address bus
questions.text: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional but the data bus is bidirectional.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Only the CPU sends addresses / chooses the location, so addresses go one way (1)
- data must go into the CPU when reading and out when writing (1)
scheme.model_answer: Only the CPU decides which location to access, so addresses travel only from the CPU; data has to move into the CPU when reading and out of it when writing.

questions.title: Reading from memory
questions.text:
The steps for reading data from memory are listed in the wrong order:

- **A** Memory puts the contents of the location on the data bus
- **B** The address is placed in the MAR and sent on the address bus
- **C** The data arrives in the MDR
- **D** A memory read signal is sent on the control bus

Write the letters in the correct order.

scheme.mark_scheme: B, D, A, C (1 each)

questions.title: Registers
questions.text: Match each register to its purpose.

right.text: Holds the address of the next instruction
Holds the address of the location to be read or written
Holds data just read from or about to be written to memory
Holds the instruction being decoded and executed
Holds the result of a calculation

scheme.mark_scheme: PC–R1, MAR–R2, MDR–R3, CIR–R4, ACC–R5.

questions.title: Correct the notation
questions.text: The fetch stage is written in register transfer notation below. Three steps contain an error. Write the correct notation for each wrong step and leave correct steps empty.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 MAR ← [PC] (1); 2 PC ← [PC] + 1 (1); 3 correct; 4 CIR ← [MDR] (1)

questions.title: The fetch stage
questions.text: Describe what happens during the **fetch** stage of the instruction cycle.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Address in PC copied to MAR / sent on address bus (1)
- PC incremented (1)
- instruction at that address copied to MDR (via data bus) then to CIR (1)
scheme.model_answer: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR, the PC is incremented, and the instruction stored at that address is read into the MDR and copied into the CIR.

questions.title: Decode and execute
questions.text: Explain what happens in the **decode** and **execute** stages.

scheme.mark_scheme: Decode: the control unit interprets the instruction / splits into opcode and operand (1). Execute: the instruction is carried out, e.g. ALU performs calculation / data moved / PC changed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Decode: the control unit splits the instruction in the CIR into opcode and operand and works out what to do. Execute: the instruction is carried out, e.g. the ALU adds or data is loaded.

questions.title: Trace LDD
questions.text:
PC = **40**. Memory address 40 contains the instruction **LDD 75**, and address 75 contains **12**.

Complete the table to show the contents of the registers after each step of fetching and executing the instruction.

questions.title: Interrupts
questions.text: Explain what an interrupt is and how the CPU deals with it during the instruction cycle.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Signal from a device / program that needs the CPU's attention (1)
- CPU checks for interrupts at the end of each cycle (1)
- saves registers / current state, runs the interrupt service routine, then restores and continues (1)
scheme.model_answer: An interrupt is a signal that a device or program needs attention. At the end of each fetch–decode–execute cycle the CPU checks for one; if found, it saves its registers, runs the interrupt service routine and then restores the registers and carries on.

questions.title: Performance factors
questions.text: Define each factor that affects the performance of the CPU.

scheme.mark_scheme: Clock speed: number of cycles the CPU performs per second (1). Word length: number of bits the CPU can process as one unit at a time (1). Bus width: number of bits a bus can carry at one time / number of lines (1)
scheme.model_answer: Clock speed: the number of clock cycles per second. Word length: the number of bits processed by the CPU in one operation. Bus width: the number of bits a bus can transfer at once.

questions.title: Clock speed
questions.text: Describe the effect of increasing the clock speed of a processor.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- More cycles per second, so instructions are executed faster (1)
- fetch–decode–execute cycle happens more times per second (1)
- more heat produced → overheating / malfunction / need cooling (1)
scheme.model_answer: More cycles happen each second, so more fetch–decode–execute cycles complete and programs run faster, but the CPU produces more heat and may overheat.

questions.title: Data bus width
questions.text: Increasing the width of the data bus increases the number of memory locations that can be addressed.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: That is the address bus. A wider data bus carries more bits per transfer.

questions.title: Cycle time
questions.text: A 64-bit data bus runs at **100 MHz** and transfers one word per cycle. Calculate the maximum data transfer rate in **MB per second** (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes).

questions.title: More cores
questions.text: Why does doubling the number of cores **not** always double the performance?

options.content: Some tasks cannot be split into parts that run in parallel
Each core has a lower clock speed than one core alone
Extra cores reduce the size of RAM

scheme.mark_scheme: A

questions.title: Choosing a processor
questions.text: Processor X: 3.0 GHz, 32-bit word, 32-bit data bus. Processor Y: 3.0 GHz, 64-bit word, 64-bit data bus.

parts.title: Word length
parts.text: Explain how the larger word length of processor Y improves performance.

scheme.mark_scheme: Processes 64 bits in one operation instead of 32 (1); larger numbers / more data per instruction so fewer instructions / cycles needed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Y can process 64 bits in one operation, so large numbers and more data are handled with fewer instructions.

parts.title: Data bus
parts.text: Explain how the wider data bus of processor Y improves performance.

scheme.mark_scheme: 8 bytes transferred at once instead of 4 (1); fewer transfers / half the time to move data between memory and CPU (1)
scheme.model_answer: It carries 64 bits (8 bytes) per transfer instead of 32, so about half as many transfers are needed to move the same data.

parts.title: Same clock
parts.text: State what the clock speed of 3.0 GHz means.

scheme.mark_scheme: 3 000 000 000 / 3 billion clock cycles per second (1)
scheme.model_answer: The clock makes 3 billion cycles every second.

questions.title: The system bus
questions.text: The system bus connects the CPU, the main memory and the I/O controllers. It is made up of a data bus, an address bus and a control bus.

parts.title: Names and purposes
parts.text: For each bus, describe its purpose and state its direction.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data: carries data / instructions between components (1); bidirectional (1). Address: carries address of the location to read / write (1); unidirectional from CPU (1). Control: carries control / timing signals e.g. read, write, clock, interrupt (1); bidirectional (1)
scheme.model_answer: Data bus: carries data and instructions; two-way. Address bus: carries the address of the memory location; one-way from the CPU. Control bus: carries signals such as memory read/write and clock; two-way.

parts.title: Writing to memory
parts.text: Explain how the three buses are used when the CPU **writes** a value to memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: Address placed on address bus (from MAR) (1); data placed on data bus (from MDR) (1); memory write signal sent on control bus (1)
scheme.model_answer: The address is sent from the MAR along the address bus, the value is sent from the MDR along the data bus, and a memory-write signal is sent along the control bus.

parts.title: Address bus width
parts.text: An address bus has **20** lines. Calculate the number of memory locations that can be addressed.

questions.title: Fetch–decode–execute
questions.text: The main function of the CPU is to execute programs using the fetch–decode–execute cycle.

parts.title: Correct the notation
parts.text: The fetch stage is described in register notation below. The given notation contains **three** errors. Write the correct notation in the last column for each wrong step.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 MAR ← [PC] (1); 2 correct; 3 MDR ← [[MAR]] (1); 4 CIR ← [MDR] (1)

parts.title: Each stage
parts.text: Explain what happens at each stage of the cycle.

scheme.mark_scheme: Fetch: next instruction copied from memory (address in PC) into CPU registers / CIR, PC incremented (1). Decode: control unit interprets the instruction / opcode and operand (1). Execute: instruction carried out by ALU / CU, e.g. calculation, data transfer, jump (1)
scheme.model_answer: Fetch: the instruction at the address in the PC is copied into the CIR and the PC is incremented. Decode: the control unit works out what the opcode and operand mean. Execute: the instruction is carried out, e.g. the ALU performs a calculation.

parts.title: Trace
parts.text: PC = **100**. Address 100 contains **ADD 60**; address 60 contains **5**; the ACC contains **10** before the instruction. Complete the values after the instruction has been fetched and executed.

parts.title: Interrupts
parts.text: Explain how an interrupt from the printer is handled within the cycle.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU checks for interrupts at the end of each cycle (1); saves registers, runs interrupt service routine, restores registers and continues (1)
scheme.model_answer: At the end of the current cycle the CPU detects the interrupt, saves its registers, runs the printer's interrupt service routine and then restores the registers to continue the program.

questions.title: CPU performance
questions.text: When developing a new processor, manufacturers consider different methods to make its performance more efficient.

parts.title: Factors
parts.text: Complete the table with **three** factors that affect the performance of the CPU. For each factor give a definition.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three factors (1 each) with matching definition (1 each): clock speed — number of cycles per second; bus width — number of bits a bus can carry at one time; word length — number of bits processed as one unit; number of cores — independent processing units; cache size — amount of fast memory in the CPU
scheme.model_answer:
| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| Clock speed | Number of cycles per second |
| Bus width | Number of bits a bus can carry at one time |
| Word length | Number of bits the CPU processes as one unit |

parts.title: Clock speed
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing the clock speed.

scheme.mark_scheme: Instructions executed at a faster rate (1); fetch–decode–execute cycles happen faster / more per second (1); increased heat may cause overheating / malfunction (1)
scheme.model_answer: More cycles per second mean instructions execute faster and more fetch–decode–execute cycles complete, but the processor gets hotter and may overheat.

summary: The components of the CPU, how data is transferred between the CPU, memory and I/O through the address, data and control buses, the registers and steps of the fetch–decode–execute cycle in register transfer notation, interrupts, and how clock speed, word length, bus width, cores and cache affect performance.

theory.title: The CPU and the system bus

blocks.content: The part of the computer that **fetches, decodes and executes** program instructions. It contains the **control unit (CU)**, the **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)**, **registers** and **cache**, and is connected to main memory and input/output devices by the **system bus**.

items.title: Control unit (CU)
items.content:
- **Decodes** instructions and **sends control signals** to the other components.
- Coordinates the **fetch–decode–execute** cycle and the movement of data along the buses.

items.title: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
items.content:
- Performs **arithmetic** (add, subtract) and **logical** operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons, shifts).
- Results are usually stored in the **accumulator (ACC)**.

items.title: Registers
items.content: - Very small, very fast storage locations **inside the CPU** that hold addresses, instructions and data being used right now.

items.title: Clock
items.content: - Sends regular **pulses** that keep all components **synchronised**; each pulse is one **clock cycle**.

blocks.content: A set of **parallel wires (lines)** on the motherboard that **connects the CPU, main memory and input/output (I/O) controllers**. Each wire carries **one bit** at a time. The system bus is made up of the **address bus**, the **data bus** and the **control bus**.

blocks.title: The three buses
rows: The **address** of the memory location (or I/O port) to be read from or written to
How **much memory** can be addressed: n lines → **2ⁿ** locations
**Bidirectional**: signals go both to and from the CPU

blocks.title: Signals on the control bus
rows: Tells memory to put the contents of the addressed location on the data bus
Tells memory to store the value on the data bus at the addressed location
Synchronises the operations of all components
A device tells the CPU it needs attention
A device asks for / is given control of the bus (e.g. for DMA)

blocks.title: Reading data from memory
items: The CPU puts the **address** in the **MAR**, and it is sent along the **address bus**.
The CU sends a **memory read** signal along the **control bus**.
Memory places the **contents** of that location on the **data bus**.
The data arrives in the **MDR**.

blocks.title: Writing data to memory
items: The **address** is placed in the **MAR** and sent along the **address bus**.
The **data** is placed in the **MDR** and sent along the **data bus**.
The CU sends a **memory write** signal along the **control bus**.
Memory stores the data at that address.

blocks.title: Why is the address bus one-way?
blocks.content: Only the **CPU** decides **which** location to use, so addresses always travel **from** the CPU. Data must travel **both** ways — into the CPU when reading and out of it when writing — so the data bus is **two-way**.

blocks.title: Special-purpose registers
rows: Holds the **address of the next instruction** to be fetched
Holds the **address** of the memory location to be read or written
**MDR** — Memory Data Register (also **MBR**, Memory Buffer Register)
Holds the **data or instruction** just read from memory or about to be written
Holds the **instruction** currently being decoded and executed
Holds the **results** of calculations by the ALU
Holds **flags**: zero, negative, carry, overflow, interrupt

blocks.content:
- **←** means "is copied into".
- **[ ]** means "**the contents of**": `[PC]` = the value stored in the PC.
- **[[MAR]]** means "the contents of the **memory location** whose address is in the MAR".
The sequence of steps the CPU repeats **for every instruction**: **fetch** the next instruction from memory, **decode** it to work out what it means, and **execute** it.

blocks.title: Fetch–decode–execute in register transfer notation
items: **MAR ← [PC]** — the address of the next instruction is copied from the PC to the MAR and sent along the **address bus**.
**PC ← [PC] + 1** — the PC is **incremented** so it points to the following instruction.
**MDR ← [[MAR]]** — a **memory read** signal is sent on the **control bus**; the instruction at that address travels along the **data bus** into the MDR.
**CIR ← [MDR]** — the instruction is copied into the CIR.
**Decode** — the **control unit** splits the instruction into **opcode** and **operand** and works out what must be done.
**Execute** — the instruction is carried out: e.g. data is loaded or stored, the **ALU** does a calculation, or a **jump** puts a new address into the PC.
**Check for interrupts**, then start the next cycle.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  F[FETCH: MAR gets PC, PC incremented, MDR gets instruction, CIR gets MDR] --> D[DECODE: control unit splits opcode and operand]
  D --> E[EXECUTE: ALU calculates, data moved, or PC changed by a jump]
  E --> I{Interrupt waiting?}
  I -- no --> F
  I -- yes --> S[Save registers, run interrupt service routine, restore]
  S --> F
blocks.caption: The instruction cycle

blocks.title: Worked example — executing LDD 50 (load the contents of address 50)
blocks.content:
PC = **20**, memory address 20 holds the instruction **LDD 50**, address 50 holds **37**.
| Step | Notation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | MAR ← [PC] | MAR = 20 |
| 2 | PC ← [PC] + 1 | PC = 21 |
| 3 | MDR ← [[MAR]] | MDR = LDD 50 |
| 4 | CIR ← [MDR] | CIR = LDD 50 |
| 5 | Decode | Opcode LDD (load direct), operand 50 |
| 6 | MAR ← 50 | MAR = 50 |
| 7 | MDR ← [[MAR]] | MDR = 37 |
| 8 | ACC ← [MDR] | ACC = 37 |

A **signal** from hardware or software (e.g. a key pressed, printer out of paper, a timer, a program error) telling the CPU that something **needs attention**. At the end of each cycle the CPU checks for interrupts; if one has a higher priority, it **saves the registers**, runs the **interrupt service routine (ISR)** and then **restores** the registers and continues.

blocks.title: Factors that affect CPU performance
rows: The **number of clock cycles per second**, measured in **hertz** (3.5 GHz = 3.5 billion cycles per second)
**More instructions** executed per second; fetch–decode–execute happens faster. But more **heat** and power — risk of overheating
The **number of bits the CPU can process as one unit** (e.g. 32 or 64 bits)
Larger numbers and **more data** processed in one operation; fewer instructions needed
The **number of bits the data bus can carry at one time**
**More data per transfer** → fewer transfers needed
The **number of lines** in the address bus
Independent processing units on one chip
Several instructions / tasks processed **in parallel** — if the software is written to use them
Very fast memory inside / near the CPU
Frequently used data and instructions found quickly → fewer slow RAM accesses

blocks.title: Worked examples
blocks.content:
- A **3 GHz** clock gives 3 000 000 000 cycles per second, so one cycle lasts 1 ÷ 3 × 10⁹ ≈ **0.33 ns**.
- Widening the data bus from **32 to 64 bits** transfers **8 bytes instead of 4** per bus cycle, so moving 1 MB takes about **half** as many transfers.
- A **64-bit** data bus at **100 MHz** can transfer 8 bytes × 100 000 000 = **800 MB per second**.
- Adding **one** line to the address bus **doubles** the addressable memory (2²⁰ = 1 MiB → 2²¹ = 2 MiB).

items.title: Limits of clock speed
items.content:
- Higher clock speed produces more **heat**; without good cooling the CPU may **malfunction** or slow itself down (**throttling**).
- **Overclocking** runs a CPU faster than its rated speed — faster, but risk of instability and damage.

items.title: Limits of more cores
items.content: - Doubling the cores does **not** double the speed: some tasks cannot be split, and cores must **share** the buses and memory.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Write the names and purposes of the buses used by the CPU. [6]**
**Data bus** (1) — carries data / instructions between the CPU, memory and I/O, in **both directions** (1). **Address bus** (1) — carries the **address** of the location data is read from or written to, **one way** from the CPU (1). **Control bus** (1) — carries **control signals** such as memory read / write, clock and interrupts (1).

**Q: The notation has errors: MDR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 2; CIR ← [MAR]. Correct them. [3]**
**MAR ← [PC]** (1); **PC ← [PC] + 1** (1); **CIR ← [MDR]** (1).

**Q: Describe the effect of increasing the clock speed. [3]**
More cycles per second, so instructions are **executed faster** (1); the fetch–decode–execute cycle happens **more often** (1); more **heat** is produced, which may cause overheating / malfunction (1).

**Q: Explain what happens in the fetch stage. [3]**
The address in the **PC** is copied to the **MAR** (1); the PC is **incremented** (1); the instruction at that address is copied into the **MDR** and then the **CIR** (1).

- Saying the **address bus** is two-way — it is **one-way** (from the CPU).
- Writing **MDR ← [PC]** — the PC's value goes to the **MAR**.
- Saying the PC holds the **current** instruction — it holds the **address** of the **next** one.
- Confusing **word length** (bits processed at once) with **bus width** (bits transferred at once).
- Saying a higher clock speed "makes the computer store more" — it makes it **process faster**.
